column2: That mare became a river and joined the Ganga, O sage; the very terrible great fire born of her the immortals called fire, which they know as the first of beings:
The waters should be known as the eldest, and you likewise as the first; among them make the eldest, the lord of waters, the ocean, your food; go as we say and eat as you please.
The fire said to the immortals, "How can I go there to the waters, unless someone takes me there to that great water?"
They said, "You yourself tell us — how may you go, O fire?" The fire said to the gods, "A maiden endowed with virtues,
placing me in a golden pitcher, should carry me to where my course lies." Hearing his words, they said to the maiden Sarasvati:
Carry this fire quickly on your head to the abode of Varuna.
Sarasvati said to the gods, "I alone cannot bear it; together with four others I could quickly carry it to the abode of Varuna."
Hearing Sarasvati's words, the gods spoke separately to the Ganga, the Yamuna, the Narmada and the Tapati.
Joined with them she carried the fire placed in the golden pitcher; bearing it on their heads, they went to the abode of Varuna,
to where the lord of gods, Somanatha, lord of the world, adorned with the moon, dwells at Prabhasa with the gods.
The five rivers with Sarasvati brought the fire there, and the great fire dwells there, drinking the water slowly.
Then all the hosts of gods said to Shiva, best of gods:
Tell us the purification for the bones, for us and for the cows.
Shiva then said to all, "By carefully bathing in the Ganga, the gods and cows are freed from that sin; there is no doubt."
And the bones from the sage's body were washed; by that very washing they attained purity there.
Where the gods were freed from sin, that holy place is Papanashana; bathing and giving there destroy the sin of brahmin-slaying.
Where the cows were purified is called Gotirtha; by bathing there the wise one obtains the fruit of a cow sacrifice.
Where the holy bones of that brahmin were, O Narada, should be known as Pitritirtha, increasing the pleasure of the ancestors.
If ashes, bones, nails or hair of any living being pass into that holy place, as long as moon, sun and stars endure,
he dwells in heaven, even if he did evil deeds. So from the Chakreshvara holy place there are three holy places, O Narada. Then the hosts of gods and the cows, purified, said to Shambhu:

We go each to our own abode; the Sun is established here. While the sun stays here, all the gods are established.
brahmapuran:110:221	O lord of the worlds, please grant permission. The Sun is the eternal self of this world, moving and unmoving.
brahmapuran:110:222	The Sun, full of the gods, has been established here by us, where the Ganga, sustainer of the world, is and where Tryambaka himself is; the dwelling of the gods would be Pratishthana, where Tryambaka is.
Taking leave of Pippalada, the gods went to their own abodes; the pippalas in course of time went to imperishable heaven.
The mighty brahmin Pippalada, establishing the place of the trees in lordship of the region, worshipped Shankara.
The sage of fierce splendour, son of Dadhichi, having obtained a wife, the daughter of Gautama, and sons, fortune and fame, the steadfast one attained heaven with his friends.
From then on that holy place is called Pippaleshvara, holy, bringing the fruit of all sacrifices, destroying sin by remembrance —
how much more by bathing and giving and by seeing the Sun! Chakreshvara and Pippalesha are the names of the god of gods;
knowing this with its secret one obtains all desires. Since the Sun was established where the gods dwell, that region is Pratishthana, dear even to the gods.
Whoever reads, hears or remembers this very holy account becomes long-lived, wealthy and righteous, and at the end, remembering Shambhu, reaches him forever.
Likewise the investiture with the sacred thread and the study of the Veda; until a twice-born studies the Veda, he is like a shudra.
Hearing these words of his son, Shurasena was greatly grieved; bringing some brahmin, he had the rites and the rest performed; the serpent, having studied the Veda, said to his father:

Arrange my marriage, O king; I desire a wife, best of kings; otherwise your duty will not be fulfilled — that is my view.
brahmapuran:111:11	A father who begets sons and does not perform all the rites according to Vedic rule has no escape from hell.
Astonished, the father said to his son of serpent form:
Who would give a maiden to one at whose very sound even brave men are terrified? Tell me, son, what shall I do?
Hearing his father's words, the clever serpent said:

There are many kinds of marriage for kings, O lord of people: abduction by force, and marriage by weapons too.
brahmapuran:111:16	When his son is married, the father has done his duty; otherwise I will die here in the Ganga; there is no doubt.
Knowing his son's resolve, the best of kings, who had no other son, summoned his ministers for the marriage and said:

My son, Nageshvara, the crown prince, a mine of virtues, virtuous, wise, brave, invincible, scorcher of foes,
brahmapuran:111:19	unequalled on earth in chariot, on elephant and with the bow — his marriage must be arranged, for I am old.
brahmapuran:111:20	Placing the burden of the kingdom on my son, I will then be free of care. As long as he takes no wife, my dear son
brahmapuran:111:21	does not give up his boyhood; therefore all of you, agreeing, devoted to my good, make efforts for the marriage.
brahmapuran:111:22	I will have no worry when my son is married; the accomplished, having placed the burden on their sons, go to the forest for austerity.
Hearing the king's words, all the ministers humbly, with joined palms and joy, said to the very radiant king:
Your son is foremost in virtue and you are famed everywhere; what is there to consult or consider about your son's marriage?
When the ministers had spoken thus, the deep best of kings did not tell the ministers that his son was a serpent; they did not know.
The king said to them again, "Which maiden would be most virtuous? Which glorious king born of a great family is the abode of virtue,
fit for alliance, brave, whose alliance is praised?" Hearing the king's words, a very wise minister,
of good family, very good, devoted to the king's interest, understanding the king's mind and knowing his signs, said this:

In the eastern land, great king, is a king named Vijaya, whose horses, elephants and jewels are beyond counting.
brahmapuran:111:30	That wise great king has eight sons, great archers; their sister Bhogavati is like another Lakshmi; she is a fitting wife for your son, O king, I say.
Hearing the old minister's words, the king replied to him:
How may his daughter become this son's wife? Tell me that.
I have perceived what is in your mind, great king; permit me to do whatever is to be done for Shurasena.
Hearing the old minister's words, he honoured him with ornaments, garments and words, and sent him with a great army.
He came to the eastern land, met the great king and honoured him with various words and means born of policy;
the very wise one, for the great king's daughter Bhogavati and the wise Naga, son of King Shurasena,
made an agreement for marriage with words both true and untrue, and honoured the king with ornaments, garments and the like.
Receiving the honour, the king then said, "I give her." Then the very wise old minister came back
and told Shurasena the matter of the marriage. Then after many days the very wise old minister,
adorned with garments and ornaments, went again quickly with a great army, accompanied by all the other counsellors,
and, for the marriage, the wise chief minister, the old one surrounded by counsellors, told the great king everything:

The son of King Shurasena, known as Naga, wise and an ocean of virtues, does not come here.
brahmapuran:111:43	The marriages of kshatriyas can be of many kinds, O king; therefore let the marriage be with weapons and ornaments, O wise one.
brahmapuran:111:44	Kshatriyas and brahmins speak true words; therefore let the marriage with weapons and ornaments be agreed.
Hearing the old minister's words, Vijaya, best of kings, accepted the words as true and the minister and the king.
The king performed Bhogavati's marriage elaborately, with a weapon according to scripture, and sent her away,
giving his own ministers, cows, gold, horses and much else; Vijaya was filled with great joy.
Taking her, the counsellors led by the old minister came to Pratishthana and presented the daughter-in-law to Shurasena;
they also conveyed Vijaya's many words, and the variegated ornaments, maidservants, garments and the rest,
and having presented them to Shurasena they were fulfilled. The ministers of Vijaya who had come with Bhogavati
the king honoured with great respect and, having done what would please Vijaya, sent them back.
Vijaya's young daughter, rich in beauty and youth, slender-waisted, constantly served her mother-in-law and father-in-law.
Bhogavati's husband, a very terrible great serpent, in a secluded, lonely house adorned with gems,
strewn with fragrant flowers, pleasant and cool, stayed there; the serpent said to his mother and father again and again:
Why does my wife, the princess, not come to me? Hearing her son's words, the serpent's mother said:
Nurse, go quickly, good woman, and tell Bhogavati, 'Your husband is a serpent'; what will she say then?
The nurse said "So be it," went to Bhogavati and, alone with her, said humbly, as never before:
I know, fortunate and gentle one, that your husband is divine; you must tell no one: he is surely a serpent, not a man.
Hearing her words, Bhogavati said this:
For human women a husband is ordinarily a man; how much more is a husband of divine race obtained by merit!
She reported Bhogavati's words in turn to the serpent, the serpent's mother and the king.
The king wept at her words, remembering the course of karma. Bhogavati too said again to that friend who had spoken before:
Show me my beloved, blessings on you; my youth is passing in vain.
Then she showed her that very terrible serpent, alone with her, on a bed strewn with fragrant flowers.
Seeing that terrible serpent, her husband adorned with jewels, with joined palms she at once spoke to her beloved:
I am blessed and favoured, whose husband is divine.
Saying this, seated on the bed, the slender one played with that serpent with serpent-like ways, with songs and embraces,
and pleased that husband with fragrant flowers and drinks. By her grace the serpent's memory returned, O sage; remembering all that fate had done, the serpent said to his beloved at night:
Though a princess, how is it that you are not afraid of me, beloved? She said, "Who can overcome what fate has ordained? The husband alone is always the refuge of women above all."
Hearing this, delighted, the Naga said to her with a smiling face:

I am pleased with your devotion; what shall I give you that you desire? By your grace, lovely one, all this memory has returned.
brahmapuran:111:72	I was cursed by the angry god of gods, the bearer of Pinaka — the mighty Naga on Maheshvara's arm, son of Shesha.
brahmapuran:111:73	I was the husband and you the wife, named Bhogavati, long ago. At Uma's words Shambhu, pleased, laughed loudly in private;
brahmapuran:111:74	and laughter came to me too, dear one, in the god's presence; then Shambhu in anger gave me this curse:
brahmapuran:111:75	'You will be a serpent in a human womb, yet possessed of knowledge.'
brahmapuran:111:76	Then Shambhu was appeased by you with me, dear one; then he said, 'While you worship me at the Gautami,
brahmapuran:111:77	I will grant knowledge to you in serpent form; then, by the grace of Bhogavati, you will be freed from the curse.'
brahmapuran:111:78	So this has come upon me and on you too, fair-faced one; therefore take me to the Gautami and worship with me.
brahmapuran:111:79	Then the curse will be removed and we shall go to Shiva again; for all who are ever distressed, Shiva alone is the highest refuge.
Hearing her husband's words, she went with her husband to the Gautami; having bathed in the Gautami, she worshipped Shiva.
Then the Lord, pleased, gave him a divine form, O sage; taking leave of his parents, the serpent was ready to go with his wife to Shiva's world. Knowing this, his wise father said:
You are the eldest and only son, heir to the kingdom; therefore rule the whole kingdom, beget many sons, and when I have gone to the supreme abode, then go to Shiva's city.
Hearing his father's words, the king of Nagas said "So be it"; obtaining the ability to take any form, he, of good vows, with his wife,
ruled the kingdom extensively with his father, mother and sons; when his father had gone to heaven, he placed his sons in his own position
and with his wife, ministers and others went to Shiva's city. From then on that holy place is famed as Nagatirtha,
where the god Nageshvara was installed by Bhogavati; bathing and giving there grant the fruit of all sacrifices.
Then the lord of the gods, pleased, for the accomplishment of the gods' task and for the benefit of the worlds, said "So be it" to the gods.
That face which is sinful, terrible and hair-raising — having cut it off with the weapons of my nails, where shall it be placed? he asked.
Then Ila said to the gods, "I cannot bear the head; I will go to Rasatala." And the ocean said,
I would dry up in a moment. Again the gods said to Shiva, "This head of Brahma must be borne by you alone, out of compassion for the worlds.
If not cut off, the worlds are destroyed; if cut off, there is such a fault." Having considered thus, Somesha then bore the head of Brahma.
Seeing that difficult deed, the gods reached the purifying Gautami and praised the lord of the worlds with love and devotion:

Having cut off with the needle of his nail-tip Brahma's very terrible head, enemy to the gods, which came to devour them, the one crowned with the crescent moon, out of compassion, bears it despite the fault of casting it away.
All the gods who were there near Brahma praised the lord of the gods, seeing that more-than-divine deed.
From then on that holy place is famed as Brahmatirtha; even today the four-faced form of Brahma stands there.
Whoever sees just the head goes to the state of Brahma. Where Rudra himself stood and cut off Brahma's head,
that is Rudratirtha; there the Sun stands visibly in the form of the gods, and therefore it is excellent;
that is called the solar holy place, granting the fruit of all sacrifices; having bathed there and seen the Sun, there is no rebirth.
The fifth head of Brahma that was cut off by Mahadeva was placed in the region of Avimukta, doing good to the gods.
Whoever sees just the head at Brahmatirtha on the Gautami's bank, and also sees Brahma's holy skull placed at Avimukta — even the slayer of a brahmin becomes pure.

I have no dharma, no devotion, no discrimination — whence compassion in me? You are the giver; therefore, O refuge, quickly place the word 'Soma' in my mind.
brahmapuran:117:15	I do not ask to be king of the gods; I ask, O Somanatha, for the presence of Shri Soma's lotus feet in the midst of my heart-lotus; consider it and do so.
brahmapuran:117:16	You know how sinful I am, yet hear my request: where the word 'Shiva' is heard, there may my dwelling be, O Somanatha.
brahmapuran:117:17	O husband of Gauri, Shankara, Somanatha, lord of the universe, treasury of compassion, self of all — where you are always praised, there may some accomplished ones dwell.
Hearing this hymn of Atreya, the Lord Hara was pleased; Bhava, maker of the universe, said to the yogin, "I am the giver of boons."
Knowledge of the self, liberation and abundant enjoyment in you, and the greatness of the holy place too — this is the boon, O one worshipped by the gods.
Saying "So be it" to him, Shambhu vanished. From then on the wise know that holy place as Atmatirtha; by bathing and giving there, liberation comes here, O Narada.
She became a river there in the Ganga; therefore that river is known by her name, Revati, bestowing beauty and good fortune.
Again he performed an anointing with various kinds of darbha grass for the attainment of a holy form; that became the river Vidarbha.
A man who bathes with faith at the confluence of the Revati and the Ganga is freed from all sins and honoured in Vishnu's world.
Likewise, whoever bathes with faith at the confluence of the Vidarbha and the Gautami, O sage, at once attains enjoyment and liberation.
On both banks there are a hundred excellent holy places, destroying all sins and granting all perfections.
Thereby came great mental torment and a loss of position hard to bear; even dharma performed with an agitated mind leads to harm
and does not accomplish its purpose; therefore it is for the untroubled. When one's own dharma is incomplete, what harm does not arise?
What happened to the two before I have also told you, sinless one. The glorious son of Ayus was the noble-minded Dhanvantari;
an obstacle was made by Tamas, and Vishnu destroyed it — such is the account of former births that has been told.
Hearing that, both were astonished and spoke to me again:
By what may that fault be countered, O best of gods?
Meditating again, I said to them: "Hear what removes the fault, the cause of all perfections, what carries across sorrowful worldly existence,
the refuge of the tormented, the bliss even of the living: go to the goddess Gautami and praise Hari and Shankara.

There is no other means of purification in the three worlds apart from those two and her." At once both went to the Gautami, O best of sages; having bathed and observed the moment, the two gods joyfully praised:

Salutation to the Fish, the Tortoise, the Boar, salutation again and again; to the god Narasimha and to Vamana, salutation again and again.
brahmapuran:122:69	Salutation to the one in horse form; Trivikrama, salutation to you; salutation to the one in the form of the Buddha, in the form of Rama, to Kalki.
brahmapuran:122:70	To Ananta, Achyuta, O Lord, to you as Jamadagnya, salutation; to you in the form of Varuna and Indra, in the form of Yama, salutation.
brahmapuran:122:71	To the supreme Lord, the god whose form is the three worlds, salutation; bearing Sarasvati in your mouth, you are all-knowing; salutation to you.
brahmapuran:122:72	You are rich in Lakshmi, since you bear Lakshmi on your breast, O sinless one; you have many arms, thighs and feet, many ears, eyes and heads; having reached you, the happy one, many have become happy.
brahmapuran:122:73	Men remain without fortune, impure and wretched only until they go for refuge to you, O Hari, ocean of compassion.
brahmapuran:122:74	Seekers of liberation call you, O Lord, the subtle supreme light of endless forms, the mere syllable Om, beyond Prakriti, whose form is consciousness, full of bliss, the whole.
brahmapuran:122:75	Those without desire who worship you here, the Lord, even with the five great sacrifices, having attained their desire beyond the ocean of worldly existence, enter your divine abode, your body.
brahmapuran:122:76	Seeing all beings with an equal mind, calm amid the six waves, casting off the fruits of action through knowledge, they enter you through meditation, O Shambhu.
brahmapuran:122:77	Not caste duties, not the Vedas and scriptures, not the yoga of meditation, not the discipline of samadhi — with devotion I bow to Rudra, Shiva, Shankara of tranquil mind, the god Soma.
brahmapuran:122:78	Even a fool, O Shambhu, by devotion to your feet attains your body made of liberation; in knowledge, sacrifices, austerities, meditations and fire offerings of great fruit —
brahmapuran:122:79	this is the highest fruit attained: devotion day and night to Someshvara; the fruit dear to every living being, seen and heard,
brahmapuran:122:80	of heaven and liberation, O dwelling of the world — this devotion to you is the stairway; for attaining your feet, the wise do not speak of a stairway.
brahmapuran:122:81	Therefore, compassionate one, let me have devotion; there is no other means than service of your form. Seeing your own greatness, O Lord, show grace to us sinners.
brahmapuran:122:82	You are gross and subtle, beginningless and eternal, father and mother, non-being and being; I bow to Someshvara, the ruler, praised thus by the Shrutis and Puranas.
Then Hari and Hara, lords of the thirty gods, pleased, said:
Choose whatever your mind desires, a boon even very rare.
Indra said to the lord of the gods, "My kingdom again and again arises and falls; let that sin be removed,
so that I may be firm in my kingdom and everything of mine be steady; if the two lords of gods are well pleased, let everything be ever steady."
Welcoming Hari's words, "So be it," the two said this, gracious, smiling, looking at them:

We two, whose nature is free from decline, without support and changeless, are the refuges of all worlds, granting enjoyment and liberation.
brahmapuran:122:89	The Gautami, great holy place of the three deities, grants what is desired; let bathing be done in her with this mantra, respectfully.
brahmapuran:122:90	Let Brihaspati perform the anointing of great Indra for auspiciousness, remembering us, for the steadiness of fortune:
brahmapuran:122:91	'Whatever good deed was done in this birth or a former one, may it all become complete; O Godavari, salutation to you.'
brahmapuran:122:92	Whoever, remembering thus, bathes in the Gautami — by the grace of us two his dharma will become complete; freed from faults committed in former births, he will become meritorious.
Saying "So be it," the lord of the gods and Dhishana were pleased; then the teacher of the dwellers of heaven performed the great anointing of Indra.
From it arose a holy river called Mangala; its confluence with the Ganga is holy and auspicious.
Praised by Indra, Vishnu, who is the world, appeared visibly; Shakra obtained from the lord of the world the earth equal to the three worlds.
He is famed there by that name, Govinda; the earth (go) equal to the three worlds was obtained by the wielder of the thunderbolt,
and given there by Hari; so Hari became Govinda. The kingship of the three worlds that Hari (Indra) obtained from Hari, O sage,
became steady through the god of gods Maheshvara. Where Brihaspati, teacher of the gods, praised Maheshvara
for the stability of the kingdom of the great-souled lord of the gods, the god there is Siddheshvara, a linga worshipped by the gods.
From then on that holy place is famed as Govinda, the confluence of the Mangala, and after that Purnatirtha,
famed as Indratirtha and known as Barhaspatya, where the god Siddheshvara and Vishnu Govinda are.
Whatever bathing, giving and acquisition of merit is done at them — know all of it to be imperishable and very dear to the ancestors.
Whoever hears, reads or daily remembers the greatness of that holy place is restored to a lost kingdom.
There are thirty-seven thousand holy places on the two banks, O tiger among sages, granting all perfections.
There is no holy place of great fruit like Purnatirtha; fruitless is the birth of the man who does not resort to it.
Who has done this painful deed to me, a good brahmin? I am called the friendly brahmin; I have committed no offence.
Hearing these words of the distressed sage, the king, motionless and dispirited, slowly approached the place.
Seeing that excellent brahmin, as if blazing with splendour, he too swooned there as if pierced by a dart.
Steadying himself by himself, the king said this:

Who are you, tiger among brahmins, and why have you come here? Tell me, a sinner; tell me the supreme expiation.
brahmapuran:123:54	The slayer of a brahmin must never be touched by those of the classes, nor even by outcastes, O wise one, nor ever be seen.
Hearing the king's words, the sage's son said:

My life-breaths will depart, so I will say something: know that in the ignorance of acting at will there is a ripening of deeds.
brahmapuran:123:57	I do not grieve for myself; but my parents are old — who will serve them, blind, with an only son?
brahmapuran:123:58	Without me, how will they live in the great forest? Ah, what is my misfortune — a failure in serving my parents
brahmapuran:123:59	has come to me today with my life gone. Alas, Fate, what have you done? Yet go there quickly, taking the pitcher,
brahmapuran:123:60	and give them water so that they do not die.
As he spoke thus, his life departed in the great forest; laying aside his bow and arrow and taking the pitcher, the king
went swiftly to where the old couple were in the great forest; the old couple that night were saying to each other:

Is he troubled or angry, or has he been devoured? Our staff has not come; what shall we do, what will become of us?
brahmapuran:123:64	There is no other son like him in all creation, who never disobeys his parents' words even when reproached.
brahmapuran:123:65	Life is harder than a thunderbolt for us who do not see him, since our breath does not quickly depart, our lives depending on him alone.
As the old couple spoke many such words in the forest, King Dasharatha slowly approached that place.
By the sound of his footsteps they thought their son had come:
Where have you come from so late, child? You are our sight and refuge. Why do you not speak — are you angry, son of the old blind couple?
Grief-stricken as if pierced by a dart, lamenting his evil deed, the king of kings, as if afraid, said to them, O Narada:
Drink water. Hearing the king's words, they said, "This speaker is not our son; tell us first who you are;
then we will drink the water." Then the king said to them:
Your son lies where the water is.
Hearing that, the distressed pair said, "Tell the truth, not otherwise." Then the king told everything as it was.
Then the old couple fell down: "Take us there; do not touch us; the sin of touching the slayer of a brahmin never perishes."
The best of kings led the old Shravana's father with his wife to where their son had fallen; touching him, they lamented:
As our death has been brought about by separation from our son, so you too, sinner, will meet death through separation from your son.
As they spoke thus, O Brahman, their life-breaths departed; then the king placed the old couple and the sage's son in the fire.
Then the grieving king went to the city, O sage, and told Vasishtha everything completely.
Vasishtha is the highest refuge of the kings of the solar line; Vasishtha, having consulted the best of brahmins, told the expiation:

Summon Galava, Vamadeva, Jabali, Kashyapa and others carefully for a horse sacrifice,
brahmapuran:123:81	and sacrifice with many horse sacrifices with abundant fees.
King Dasharatha performed horse sacrifices with the brahmins; meanwhile a bodiless voice spoke there:
King Dasharatha's body has become pure; he will be fit for social dealings and will have sons; by the grace of his eldest son the king will become sinless.
Then after many days, from Rishyashringa, lord of sages, for the accomplishment of the gods' task, sons like the gods were born:
Rama of Kausalya, Lakshmana and Shatrughna of Sumitra, and the very wise Bharata of Kaikeyi.
All were wise, dear, and obedient to the king. The sage Vishvamitra, a lord of creatures, came to the king
and asked for Rama and Lakshmana, O wise one, for the protection of his sacrifice, the sage knowing their greatness.
The old king, who had obtained sons after long, said "No":

By great good fortune, somehow, in my old age, O sage, these two boys were born to me, giving a flood of joy.
brahmapuran:123:90	I will give this kingdom with my body, but not these two sons.
Then Vasishtha said to King Dasharatha:
The Raghus have never been taught to refuse a request, O king.
With difficulty the king said to Rama and Lakshmana:
Protect the sacrifice of the brahmin sage Vishvamitra.
Saying this, sighing hotly, his lips parched, the upholder of scripture handed his two sons to Vishvamitra.
Saying "So be it" to Dasharatha and bowing again and again, the two joyfully went with Vishvamitra to protect the sacrifice.
Then the sage, delighted, joyfully gave both of them the great knowledge of Maheshvara, headed by the science of archery,
the scriptural, the missile and the worldly sciences, the science of chariots, of elephants, of horses, of the mace, and the invoking and releasing of mantras.
Having obtained all knowledge, Rama and Lakshmana killed Tataka in the forest for the good of the forest-dwellers.
They freed Ahalya from her curse by the touch of a foot, and killed the Rakshasas who came to destroy the sacrifice.
Skilled in knowledge, bows in hand, they protected the sacrifice. When the great sacrifice was over, Vishvamitra, lord of sages,
went with the king's two sons to see Janaka. There among the kings the prince displayed a wonder:
Rama with Saumitri showed the archery approved by his teacher; pleased, Janaka gave Sita, Lakshmi not born of a womb.
Likewise for Lakshmana and his younger brother Bharata, for Shatrughna, Bharata and the others, following the counsel of Vasishtha and the rest,
the glorious King Dasharatha performed the marriages, O sage. Then after many days, when he was giving the kingdom to him
with the consent of all the people and the teacher, Kaikeyi, impelled by the ill fate in the form of Manthara and filled with jealousy,
set up an obstacle and the banishment to the forest; and the king did not give that kingdom to Bharata.
Keeping his father's word true, Rama entered the great forest with Sita and with Saumitri,
and by his own virtues he entered the pure minds of the good. When Rama had gone out, consecrated for dwelling in the forest,
with Lakshmana and Sita, free from thirst for the kingdom, overcome with great grief for Rama, Saumitri and the virtuous Sita,
and remembering the brahmin's curse, King Dasharatha, grief-stricken, gave up his life.
By the ripening of his deeds the king was taken by Yama's servants; for that king, O wise one, among the unmoving and moving,
in Yama's abode there were many hells beginning with Tamisra, O Narada, terrible, fearsome and many.
Cast into those hells one after another, the king was cooked, cut, ground and crushed,
dried, bitten, burned again and submerged; the king was tormented in such terrible hells.
Rama too, going along the road, came to Chitrakuta; there three years passed, O wise one.
Again he went south into the Dandaka forest, famed in the three worlds, the most meritorious of lands.
He entered that great forest, terrible and frequented by Daityas, abandoned by the sages out of fear of them; killing the Daityas and Rakshasas,
wandering in the Dandaka forest, he made it fit for the sages to frequent. There I shall tell this story; hear it carefully, O Narada.
Slowly Rama went up to five yojanas and reached the Gautami, while the king was in hell.
Yama said to his servants: "Rama, son of Dasharatha, is going toward the Gautami; his wise father —
draw the king out of hell without doubt. As long as Rama goes across the Gautami for five yojanas,
so long his father must not be cooked in hell. If the messengers do not carry out this holy word of mine,
then all of you will sink in terrible hell. Whatever supreme power of Shiva is said to be inseparable from him,
the good call that very Gautami, in the form of water; she is honoured and worshipped by Hari, Brahma and Mahesha.
The sin of transgressing her cannot be crossed by anyone. Even the son of a sinner who remembers the Ganga
comes out of many hellish fortresses and attains liberation — how much more such a son staying near the Gautami,
whose father no one can torment in hell!" Hearing the words of the lord of the southern quarter, Yama's servants
lifted the king of Ayodhya being tormented in hell out of the terrible hell and said these words:
Blessed are you, tiger among kings, whose son is such; by whom is rest obtained here and hereafter except through a good son?
Rested, the king slowly spoke to the servants:
While being tormented again and again in terrible hells, how was I quickly drawn out? You should tell me that.
One of them, of calm mind, said to the king:

This is carefully kept secret in the Vedas, scriptures, Puranas and the like; yet it is revealed to you — the power of a son and a holy place.
brahmapuran:123:135	Rama, your glorious son, has come to the bank of the Gautami; therefore you have been drawn out of terrible hell, best of men.
brahmapuran:123:136	If Rama with Lakshmana remembers you there at the Gautami and, having bathed, offers you rice-balls and the rest, best of kings, then you will be freed from all sins and go to heaven.
Going there, I will tell your words to my two sons; you alone are my refuge; please give me leave.
Hearing the king's words, Yama's servants out of compassion gave him leave, and the king went to his two sons,
having taken on a terrible body of torment, sighing again and again, ashamed at seeing himself and remembering the deed he had done.
Roaming at will, Raghava reached the Ganga; resorting to the bank of the Gautami, Rama and Lakshmana
with Sita of Videha bathed duly; there was no food to eat or chew on the Gautami's bank
that day for them staying among the dwellers of the Gautami's bank; seeing that, his brother Lakshmana, grieved, said to Rama:
We are the two sons of Dasharatha, and your strength is such, yet we who dwell on the Ganga's bank have no food.

Brother, what has been ordained cannot be otherwise; on the earth full of food, we long for food.
brahmapuran:123:145	O Saumitri, surely we have not offered oblations into the mouths of brahmins; those who out of contempt do not satisfy or honour the gods of the earth,
brahmapuran:123:146	O Lakshmana, are always born hungry. Having bathed and worshipped the gods, the fire should be offered oblations; then in due time God will provide food for us.
As the brothers talked thus, seeing the course of karma, King Dasharatha slowly approached that place.
Seeing him, Lakshmana quickly said, "Stop, stop!" drawing his bow in anger: "Are you a Rakshasa or a Danava?
Seeing him come near again: "Go away, go away; here Rama, son of Dasharatha, the righteous king, is present — see:
devoted to his elders, true to his promise, servant of gods and brahmins, able to protect the three worlds — where Raghava is,
there is no entry for sinners like you; if you enter, sinner, you will meet death."
Hearing his son's words, he softly called with his voice and, face downcast, with joined palms, spoke to his daughter-in-law and sons, reflecting again and again on the course of evil deeds:
I am King Dasharatha; my sons, hear my words. Beset by three brahmin-slayings, I have come to sorrow; see my body cut and cast into hells.
Then Rama with joined palms, with Sita and Lakshmana, all bowed to the ground and said these words:
Of what deed is this the fruit, father, best of kings?
And he told as it happened the three brahmin-slayings:
There is no expiation anywhere, my sons, for the slayers of brahmins.
Then, overcome with great grief, all fell to the ground; remembering the king, the forest-dwelling, their mothers and father,
the coming of sorrow, the course of karma and the fall into hell, the prince swooned; seeing the prince unconscious, Sita said:

Great souls like you do not grieve when misfortune comes; they think of a remedy, divine or human.
brahmapuran:123:161	By those who grieve for a thousand ages calamity is not crossed; the discerning never fall into bewilderment here.
brahmapuran:123:162	What use is this fruitless grief here, O lord of people? Give me the first slaying, which was very terrible —
brahmapuran:123:163	for the brahmin who was killed though innocent, devoted to his parents, of holy conduct, master of the Vedas and their limbs — I will perform the expiation for that sin
brahmapuran:123:164	according to scripture; do not grieve, you two. Let Lakshmana take the second slaying, and you the other.
These firm, righteous words were spoken by Sita; both said "So be it"; then Dasharatha said:
You are the daughter of Janaka, knower of Brahman, not born of a womb, the wife of Rama; what wonder that you speak what is fitting?
